facts.note: Narrative §6.3 verbatim: 'The Council is expected to be in an under-borrowed position as at 31 March 2026. summary.text:
Exeter is a small-to-mid-size district on the PWLB side of the sector — the whole £172m of external debt is PWLB, split £89.88m General Fund and £72.244m HRA at 31 December 2025 (paper §3.2). Nine loans in total: eight long-dated (£162.124m at ~2.34% weighted) plus one £10m short-term slot. CFR at 31 March 2026 is expected to be £237.477m (paper §6.1), rising to £242.393m by March 2027 as capital expenditure is incurred. The balance-sheet identity ties: £237.477m CFR less £162.124m external long-term borrowing leaves £75.353m of internal borrowing — the figure the paper itself prints in the §6.2 table.

Our PWLB price book at today's snapshot (14 August 2026) reconciles to the pound-ish. We hold the same nine loans at £171.668m weighted 2.4687%; the £456k principal delta against the paper's 31 December figure is annuity amortisation over the ~8 months in between. The only substantive change is on the short-term slot: the £10m PWLB at 4.87% maturing 12 March 2026 has run off, and a fresh £10m short-term at 4.56% maturing 17 March 2027 has been drawn — a like-for-like rollover at 31bp lower. That is the mechanism §6.5 anticipates.

What is most distinctive is the value of the locked-in position. Priced against today's certainty curve, the nine live loans carry an indicative discount of £67.274m against £171.297m of balance — 39.3% of principal. Four long-dated loans do nearly all the work: the £41.44m annuity mat 2071 at 1.78% (−£19.4m), the £56.884m HRA settlement mat 2062 at 3.48% (−£18.1m), the £32.93m annuity mat 2069 at 1.80% (−£14.9m), and the £15.36m HRA loan mat 2070 at 1.31% (−£10.5m). The £15.36m at 1.31% is the deepest single line — indicative settlement is about 31% of face today. That is what a 1.31% coupon does against a 50-year certainty curve at 6.08%. Indicative only — only the DMO can quote — and the replacement cost is what a real repayment decision would turn on.

The MUFG rate forecast (Appendix A §2) is a dated, falsifiable assumption worth flagging. At 22 December 2025 MUFG had certainty rates falling across all tenors through 2026 and 2027 — 10-yr from 5.20% at Mar-26 to 4.80% by Mar-27, 25-yr from 5.80% to 5.50%. Eight months on the market has moved the other way at the long end: today's 10-yr is 5.83%, 20-yr 6.38%. Bank Rate has held at 3.75% (broadly on track) and the short end has drifted a little lower, but the long-end forecast has been overtaken by roughly 60-90 basis points across 10-year to 50-year tenors. That is worth putting alongside the paper's §6.9 caveat ('with long-term rates not forecast to reduce in the near future, any such short-term savings will need to be balanced against potential longer-term costs') for the mid-year report.

The financing-costs-to-net-revenue ratio (GF 19-20%, HRA ~8%) sits mid-distribution across the file — not a distress signal. The CCLA-LAMIT £5m holding falls inside the IFRS 9 statutory override which currently ends 31 March 2029; paper doesn't comment on the override cliff, worth carrying forward. Neither the covering report nor either appendix carries a report-author email; the S151 David Hodgso[n] and the report author Kayleigh Searle (Finance Lead - Capital) are named on the covering report but the general enquiries line is a committee-clerk address, not a treasury contact. Note is drafted-needs-address per the pipeline convention.

officer.body:
Hi,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 that went to Executive on 3 February and to Council on 24 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A reconciliation first. Our PWLB file today holds the same nine loans your §3.2 schedule shows at 31 December: £171.668m at 2.47% weighted, against your £172.124m at roughly 2.49%. The £456k principal gap is amortisation on the six annuity loans over the eight months in between. The only line that has changed is the short-term one — the £10m PWLB at 4.87% maturing 12 March has run off, and a fresh £10m short-term at 4.56% maturing 17 March 2027 has been drawn in its place, five days later. A clean like-for-like rollover at 31 basis points cheaper. Your balance-sheet identity also ties: CFR of £237.477m less external long-term borrowing of £162.124m leaves £75.353m internal, the number your §6.2 table prints.

What's most distinctive in the file is the value of the long-term anchor. Priced against today's certainty curve (14 August, notice 314/26 PM) the nine live loans on our file carry an indicative discount of £67.27m against £171.30m of balance — roughly 39% below par, and one of the larger locked-in positions in what we've read. Four long-dated loans do nearly all the work: the £41.4m annuity maturing December 2071 at 1.78%, the £56.9m HRA settlement maturing March 2062 at 3.48%, the £32.9m annuity maturing September 2069 at 1.80%, and the £15.4m HRA loan maturing April 2070 at 1.31%. The £15.4m at 1.31% is the deepest single line — indicative settlement is roughly 31% of face today, or about £4.8m against £15.4m outstanding. That is what a 1.31% coupon does against a 50-year certainty curve at 6.08%. Every council's book is priced daily on this basis at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Indicative only, of course, and only the DMO can quote; we model no MRP or accounting treatment on top.

The other feature worth flagging is the MUFG forecast at Appendix A §2. Their view at 22 December 2025 had Bank Rate falling to 3.50% by mid-2026 and 3.25% by December, and PWLB certainty rates falling across all tenors — 10-year going from 5.20% at March 2026 down to 4.80% by March 2027, 25-year from 5.80% to 5.50%, 50-year from 5.60% to 5.30%. Eight months on the picture has moved the other way. Bank Rate is still 3.75%; the two cuts MUFG expected by year-end haven't landed. Today's 10-year certainty is 5.83% against their 5.00% for mid-2026, and 50-year is 6.08% against their 5.50%. Roughly 60 to 90 basis points above the December view at the long end, and Bank Rate 25 to 50 basis points above what they had for now. Your §6.9 already anticipates this risk ('with long-term rates not forecast to reduce in the near future, any such short-term savings will need to be balanced against potential longer-term costs'), so it is more a data point for the mid-year report than a surprise. The full curve and the SONIA path it runs off are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

One small piece of context from the wider file. July's sector PWLB drawings across all councils were £368m from just 19 borrowers — a thin month. The breakdown by tenor and by council is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. It gives a sense of what shape of borrowing has been going through and what the sector has been paying since your strategy was set. On our side we hold PWLB only, so if you have any LOBO, bank or market debt outside PWLB none of the above touches it — though your §3.2 schedule reads as all-PWLB, which matches our file.

Four courses fit. Reading the PWLB certainty curve covers the mechanics of what the MUFG table quotes and what has moved since. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Code updates — your Appendix B is the LB chart the paper references at §8.2 but not the underlying tabulation, so this is one to watch as the Code lands. IFRS 9 statutory override — the 2029 cliff matters given the £5m CCLA-LAMIT holding on §3.1. And Members' introduction to treasury is the one to point Cabinet at ahead of the next strategy cycle. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
